title: ASEAN in the Emerging AI Power Order
subtitle: Distributed National Nodes, Overlapping Technological Systems, and Strategic Autonomy
full_title: ASEAN in the Emerging AI Power Order: Distributed National Nodes, Overlapping Technological Systems, and Strategic Autonomy

creators.name: Wu, Shaoyuan
creators.affiliation: Global AI Governance and Policy Research Center, EPINOVA LLC

publisher_unit: Global AI Governance and Policy Research Center
description: This policy brief examines ASEAN’s place in the emerging AI power order as a distributed regional coordination and overlap environment rather than a unified AI power. It distinguishes AI National Power at the member-state level, AI Boundary Power at specific controller–target–interface relations, Boundary Autonomy as the ability to preserve functions through credible alternatives, and Systemic Influence as a separate outcome requiring persistent, sufficiently broad, and credibly attributable effects. The brief compares the differentiated functional roles of ASEAN’s eleven members, analyzes four regional mechanisms—aggregation, interoperability, option-set expansion, and mediation—and examines overlap among U.S., Chinese, domestic, Japanese, Korean, European, Indian, and Gulf-linked technological systems. A diagnostic Malaysia–Singapore advanced-compute case illustrates how locally held legal and regulatory interfaces can become strategically consequential without creating a unified ASEAN enforcement regime. The brief concludes that ASEAN’s strategic relevance lies in interoperable pluralism: preserving multiple workable connections, strengthening nationally controlled interfaces, and converting coordination and investment into operational interoperability, credible alternatives, and durable local capability.
abstract: Southeast Asia is often portrayed as a contested space between U.S. and Chinese artificial-intelligence ecosystems. This brief argues that ASEAN is best understood as a distributed regional coordination and overlap environment. AI National Power remains attributable to member-state systems and their usable, mobilizable functions. AI Boundary Power is relational; Boundary Autonomy describes a target's credible ability to switch, substitute, bypass, or internalize at an interface; and Systemic Influence requires a separate showing of persistent, sufficiently broad, credibly attributable effects. Four mechanisms warrant attention: aggregation of complementary nodes, interoperability among systems, expansion of credible national options, and mediation across external technology and governance agendas. The immediate policy opportunity is interoperable pluralism: preserving multiple workable connections, securing nationally controlled interfaces, and converting investments into capabilities that can operate across organizational and technological boundaries.

methodology.framework_name: ANP–ABP–Boundary Autonomy–Systemic Influence Regional Coordination Framework
methodology.geographic_scope: ASEAN’s eleven member states, including Timor-Leste following its admission in October 2025.
methodology.evidentiary_scope: Evidence cutoff: September 30, 2026. Functional roles are overlapping and time-indexed. Supported, Bounded/Function-Specific, Formation-Stage, and Evidence-Constrained labels qualify claims rather than rank countries.
methodology.core_problem: How differentiated national AI capabilities, locally administered boundary rights, and overlapping external technological systems interact through ASEAN coordination without being collapsed into a single regional stock of AI power.

regional_mechanisms.name: Aggregation
regional_mechanisms.description: Regional complementarity without proof of joint mobilization.

regional_mechanisms.name: Interoperability
regional_mechanisms.description: Reduced coordination costs across national rules and technological systems while enforcement remains national.

regional_mechanisms.name: Option-set expansion
regional_mechanisms.description: Potential strategic advantage from multiple suppliers, hosting sites, model ecosystems, and legal pathways, conditional on demonstrated substitution.

regional_mechanisms.name: Mediation
regional_mechanisms.description: ASEAN’s recurring institutional role across external technology and governance forums without implying equidistance or enforceable regional control.

key_findings: ASEAN is a consequential coordination environment rather than a unified AI power.
Member-state functions matter more than a single readiness ranking.
Technological overlap is not equivalent to geopolitical alignment.
Interoperability may increase strategic options without pooling sovereignty.
Selected advanced-compute interfaces show consequential local boundary control.
No current evidence establishes region-wide Systemic Influence.
The 2030 policy test is conversion rather than institutional symbolism.
policy_recommendations: Turn regional AI guidance into verifiable interoperability.
Measure nationally usable capacity rather than announced infrastructure.
Convert hosting and industrial investment into domestic learning.
Preserve multiple external partnerships while distinguishing control rights.

pathways_2030.name: Interoperable pluralism
pathways_2030.description: Regional guidance supports recurring cross-border functions, meaningful substitutability, and differentiated partnerships.

pathways_2030.name: Parallel expansion
pathways_2030.description: Infrastructure and policy investments proliferate while systems remain administratively or technically disconnected.

pathways_2030.name: Fragmented dependence
pathways_2030.description: Critical interfaces become concentrated or incompatible and external restrictions force costly adaptation.

tests_2030: Number and functional significance of cross-border arrangements actually operating.
Demonstrated portability or recovery of priority AI services after provider interruption.
Transparent evidence of domestic value capture from hosted infrastructure.
Interoperability of governance and compliance procedures without suppression of national experimentation.
Inclusion of lower-capacity members in operational rather than merely ceremonial regional programs.
